# 1\. Context

*This section is **informative**.*

# 2\. Information Model

## 2.1 Overview

*This section is **informative**.*

* The information model is based on the [ODRL](https://www.w3.org/TR/odrl-model/), with a number of refinements and extensions.   
* The basis of the information model is an inventory of **Rules.** An alternative label for Rules is **Provisions**.  
* The **Rules** apply to a **Work** (**Asset** in ODRL), and **Assets** can be grouped in **Asset Collections**. Alternative labels include **CreativeWork** ([schema.org](http://schema.org)), while some contexts such as [Dublin Core](https://dublincore.org/) and [DCAT](https://dcat.org/) have narrower concepts that are included conceptually in the **Work**/ **Asset** concept.  
* These **Rules** have classifications and typologies, as follows:  
  * **Rules** are one of three subclasses that are defined in a vocabulary, with each concept provided with an IRI. The concepts can have alternative labels and descriptions and could reference external IRIs defined elsewhere in the web. These types are:  
    * **Permissions**: rights inherent to the rights holder that are also available to the user of the **Work**.  
    * **Prohibitions** (alternative **Restrictions**): rights, actions, or end uses that are not afforded or transferred to users of the **Work**.  
    * **Obligations** (alternative **Duties**): actions that must be performed by the user of the **Work**.  
  * In the context of OpenREL, **Rules** can be classified with a **Purpose**, and these can be one or more of the following:  
    * **Licence** rules: these rules pertain to intellectual property rights, and are usually associated with the creator(s) of the **Work**.  
    * **Access** rules: primarily aimed at protecting the rights of the subjects of study in research, and extending to data based on the subject.  
    * **Process** rules: other rights and responsibilities applicable to end users, curators, repositories, and archives, aimed to determine allowable actions by these agents or e.g. obligations and restrictions imposed by legislation, regulations, best practices, or applicable policies.  
    * **Policy** rules: statements of intent, desirable outcomes, or limitations to use and management of works that are defined in policy.  
* Refinements and extensions include:  
  * ODRL considers a collection of **Rules** to be a **Policy**, but there are special cases of such collections. Specifically, based on the **Purpose** of the **Rules** collection, it can be a **Licence**, **Access** Conditions, or **Process** Rules, with the default being a **Policy** if the collection is ***not*** one of the special cases.   
  * **Rules** collections can be gathered in one document with separate sections defining any specialisations. Specialisations can also be included by reference to an external document defining the collection of Rules that are applicable.  
  * There are a number of **Agents** involved in the ecosystem, each with specific roles and responsibilities, some of which are defined in legislation such as the GDPR. These agents are similar to those defined in other contexts, such as for example DCAT-AP, and in the ODRL information model, these agents can be encoded as a special case of **Party Collections.** The agents identified to date are included in a registry, with each concept having a unique IRI, a label and possibly alternative labels, a description, and optionally references to one or more external definitions of the same concept via an IRI.  
  * A rule can be applicable to one or more agents, and agents can be subject to one or more rules. A rule has no meaning if it is not assigned to at least one agent.  
  * The **Agents** identified to date are:  
    * **Creator** (alternative **Contributor**): the legal person(s) involved in creation of the work and by default the **Rights Holder**.  
    * **Rights Holder** (alternative **Owner**): the legal person(s) that hold the intellectual property rights to the work.  
    * **End User**: the legal person that intends to reuse the work. This agent overlaps with the definition of responsibilities associated with the **Processor** in GDPR legislation.   
    * **Depositor**: the legal person that acts as the depositor of the work in a repository or archive, and usually one of the **Creators** or **Rights Holders**. By default, this person is also responsible for adjudicating access requests (**Controller**).  
    * **Controller**: The legal person responsible for implementation and monitoring of access requests and other legal obligations applicable to the work. By default, this is the **Depositor,** with some rules applicable to the **Curator**.  
    * **Curator**: the legal person that takes custody of the work for purposes of publication, dissemination, and long-term preservation. The **Curator** typically serves as a proxy for the **Controller** in respect of access request adjudication if the **Controller** is unavailable, not capable of adjudication, or explicitly transfers the responsibility to the **Curator**. The **Curator** is also responsible for ensuring compliance with Licence, Process, and Policy rules, and also acts in some cases as a **Processor** in terms of GDPR.  
  * A **Rule** **Collection** can be named and reused, and each collection has a unique identifier (IRI) . A **Rule Collection** is equivalent to an ODRL **Policy**.  
  * A **Rule** **Collection** can be applied to an **Asset** or an **Asset Collection**.  
  * A **Rule** can have one or more **Purpose** classifications: **Licence** rule, **Access** rule, **Process** rule, and/ or **Policy** rule. Except in special cases, all **Licence**, **Access**, and **Process** rules will link to at least one **Policy** rule, which indicates how a policy provision is implemented.  
  * A **Rule** **Collection** can apply to more than one **Asset Collection**, and an **Asset Collection** can have more than one **Rule** **Collection** assigned. For any given work (**Asset**) or **Asset Collection**, the following can be applicable:  
    * A **Licence** Collection (mandatory) \[1..1\], defining the scope of rules applicable to the **Rights Holder**, and indicating which of these apply to other agents (usually the **End User**).  
    * Optionally, 1 or more **Access** Collections \[0..n\] applicable to the work, and typically defining the rules for the **End User** agent.     
    * Optionally, 1 or more **Process** Collections \[0..n\] applicable to the work, and typically defining the rules for the **Depositor** and **Curator** agent.

In summary: Figure 2.1 shows the main OpenREL extensions to ODRL graphically. The main focus is on qualifying a **Rules Collection** (ODRL **Policy**) in terms of its **Purpose** (**Licence**, **Access** Rules, **Process** Rules, or an explicit **Policy**), and to align the definition of **Party Collection**s with **Agents** defined in the RDMI landscape. 

## 2.2 Content Specification

The OpenREL content based on the information model is hosted in the OpenREL Knowledge Base. The content is described in the Annexures to this document, and will change over time as amendments and new releases of the knowledge base are made.

Content is grouped into the following logical sections:

1. **Schema Definition** (‘Schema’) \- the RDF and SHACL definitions of schema patterns for specific classes and concept schemes, and a definition of the properties defined for each class and concept scheme.  
2. **Vocabularies** (‘Vocabs’): The code lists and vocabularies, expressed as RDF concept schemes, to be used in OpenREL. These resources are divided into subgroups:  
   1. **openrel**: vocabularies that have been defined explicitly by OpenREL.  
   2. A wide array of **other vocabularies** (e.g. ODRL, DALICC, IDSC, etc.) that are cached in the Knowledge Base for convenience, and, in some cases, extended by OpenREL.

# 3\. Implementation

*This section is **informative**.*

The OpenREL Information Model allows one to implement the definition of rights, access conditions, processing obligations and restrictions, and policy formulations in a number of ways, as described below in a non-comprehensive list of use cases. The implementations make use of classes and their instances defined in the OpenREL namespace, deployed in a Github repository.

## 3.1 The OpenREL Namespace

The EOSC Beyond project will establish a namespace for redirection to OpenREL class, property, and concept definitions and provide a target registry for inventories of Agents (Party Collections), Rules, Asset Collections, Policies, and Constraints. This namespace is used to provide a uniform IRI source and definition for these classes, and extends and refines classes defined elsewhere (ODRL, CCREL, etc.).

## 3.2 Deployment

The OpenREL registry and knowledge base is deployed in a Git-based repository, with the following advantages:

1. Curation is performed by the repository owner(s) by way of evaluation, acceptance, modification, or rejection of pull requests.  
2. These pull requests can deal with modifications and edits to existing registry content, or request new instances of the classes managed in the repository.  
3. Public participation via Git repository accounts is available to anyone.  
4. Version control is robustly provided by the Git repository platform.

## 3.3 Encoding Examples

The examples below illustrate the flexibility expected from the OpenREL specifications and schema. These can be used as tests to confirm that the Information Model will be able to encode each example.

### 3.3.1 Definition of a New Rule

Any interested party can construct a new **Rule** definition based on a template for **Rules**, and submit the new **Rule** as a pull request to the Git repository. The request will be evaluated by the curators of the registry, and accepted, rejected, or referred back with suggested modifications. The **Rule** is validated against the schema for compliance. If accepted, the new **Rule** is publicly available with a unique IRI, and is added to the OpenREL namespace. Similarity, equivalence, and relations to other Rules are determined by human curators.

### 3.3.2 Definition of one or more Policies

Any interested party can encode and submit a **Policy** as a pull request. Such a policy is represented by a **Rules Collection**, and is applicable to a specific **Asset** or **Asset Collection**. The **Policy** can be one of the specific categories defined by the OpenREL **Purpose** vocabulary (**Licence**, explicit **Policy**, **Access** Rules, **Process** Rules). The request will be evaluated by the curators of the registry, and accepted, rejected, or referred back with suggested modifications. The **Policy** is validated against the schema for compliance. If accepted, the new **Policy** is publicly available with a unique IRI, and is added to the OpenREL namespace. In many cases, formulation of a new **Policy** will require formulation of one or more new **Rules**.

### 3.3.3 Definition of an Existing Licence

An existing **Licence**, for example the [CC BY 4.0 Licence](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/deed.en), can be encoded by referencing a set of **Rules** and associated **Constraints**, as applicable to one or more **Agents**. A **Licence** is a **Rules Collection** that is a special case of a **Policy** (in terms of ODRL), and as such, is tagged with the applicable **Purpose** vocabulary concept. Any interested party can encode and submit a **Licence** as a pull request. The request will be evaluated by the curators of the registry, and accepted, rejected, or referred back with suggested modifications. The **Licence** is validated against the **Policy** schema for compliance. Even though OpenREL will provide an IRI for the new **Licence** by default, such a **Licence** is unlikely to have its preferred IRI based on the OpenREL IRI, since well-known IRIs often exist already (for example from [SPDX](https://spdx.dev/), and available via the [EDEN Licence Facade Service](https://lfs.labs.dansdemo.nl/docs#/) \- see section 3.4).

### 3.3.4 Definition of a Custom/ New Licence

Custom or new **Licences**, again as a special case of the **Policy** class, can be implemented in two ways: by referencing an existing **License** and adding **Rules** to further constrain the **Permissions**, adding **Obligations**, and adding **Prohibitions** from the inventory of **Rules**, or by creating a **Licence** *de novo* from **Rules**. The latter process can easily be based on an existing **Licence** too by starting with a copy of a **Licence** that closely resembles the desired scope of **Rules**. Any interested party can encode and submit a **Licence** as a pull request. The request will be evaluated by the curators of the registry, and accepted, rejected, or referred back with suggested modifications. The **Licence** is validated against the **Policy** schema for compliance. Two additional validations are required \- that the new Licence does not correspond exactly to an existing Licence, and that the Rules included in the **Licence** and/or indirectly referenced in an existing **Licence** are all compatible. Moreover, it may be useful to point out near similarity to existing **Licences** in an attempt to limit the number of defined Licences (see section 3.4).  OpenREL will provide an IRI for the new **Licence** via the EDEN Licence Facade Service, which in turn requires a pull request to SPDX. This approach avoids creating multiple authoritative sources of Licence IRIs.

### 3.3.5 Definition of Access Conditions

**Access** Conditions can be encoded as a special case of the ODRL **Policy** class by tagging it with the **Access** concept from the **Purpose** vocabulary. One or more **Rules** with applicable **Constraints** are linked to the **Access** conditions, and indicating which **Agents** are implicated by or responsible for the **Rules**. Any interested party can encode and submit **Access** Conditions as a pull request. The request will be evaluated by the curators of the registry, and accepted, rejected, or referred back with suggested modifications. The **Access** Conditions is validated against the **Policy** schema for compliance. OpenREL will provide an IRI for the new **Access** Conditions collection. 

### 3.3.6 A More Complex Example

In many applications, it will be required to provide access to machine-readable **Rules** that cover **License**, **Access**, and **Process** provisions via a single entry point. It could also be useful to link to machine-readable **Policy** provisions simultaneously.  These **Rules** may be captured in different **Policy** encodings, and the majority of metadata schema will allow only a single reference to a set of **Rules** \- typically a ‘licence’. Moreover, even if metadata schema allow references to other provisions (for example ‘access conditions’, these elements are much less standardised and prevalent than the ‘licence’ element. As indicated in section 2, a simplified mechanism is provided for predictable access to all relevant Policy elements. Using this mechanism, a Policy may include

* A ‘**Policy**’ section that points via IRI to one or more specific **Policies** encoded separately;  
* A ‘**Licence**’ section that points to a standardised **Licence** encoded separately, for example a CC BY 4.0 **Licence**;  
* Additional **Access** conditions encoded locally in a section by referencing one or more **Rules**;  
* And a **Process** section that locally encodes **Rules** applicable to **Process** provisions.

Figure 3.3.6.1 shows an example of such a complex implementation.

## 3.4 Limiting Proliferation

There will be a natural tendency towards definition of new **Licences**, **Access** Conditions, **Process** Rules, or **Policies**.  This may not be desirable, depending on the context:

* If a new **Policy** (**Licence**, **Access** Conditions, **Policy**, or **Process** Rules) is defined for an **Asset Collection**, limiting diversity is an objective. The community benefits from having as few versions as possible of ‘Access Conditions for Endangered Species Data’, ‘Process Rules for Personal Data’ or ‘Disclosure Risk Policy’.  
* If, on the other hand, a new **Policy** is defined directly for an individual **Asset** (for example in Life Sciences, where an individual may define a custom set of **Permissions**, **Obligations**, and **Prohibitions** applicable to  personal genetic data),  such object-level customisation is unavoidable. 

In both instances, a relation is defined between a **Policy** (a set of **Rules**) and either an **Asset** (identified by an object PID), or an **Asset Collection** (usually defined in the OpenREL Namespace). 

The ODRL Information Model makes provision for directly linking **Rules** to **Assets**, but linking **Rules** as a named set of **Rules** to individual **Assets** includes the possibility of reusing the set in cases where this is possible, limiting the number of relations in the graph.

## 3.5 Integration with SPDX and the EDEN Licence Facade Service

Many **Licences** already have commonly used IRIs, which are usually the URL associated with a human-readable representation of the **Licence**. A **Licence**, however, typically could also have a machine-readable representation, as well as a legal code representation. These representations are not always reliably available from the source or accessible to machines. The [SPDX Licence Registry](https://spdx.org/licenses/), hosted as a [Github repository](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-data), addresses this issue, while also providing stable IRIs for most licences from one service. SPDX is focused on software licences, though, and may not provide references to all commonly used data licences. SPDX also does not store other collections of Rules, such as machine-readable Policies, Access Conditions, or Process Rules. SPDX may also reject pull requests for new licences contributed on behalf of the research data management community.

The [EDEN Licence Facade Service](https://lfs.labs.dansdemo.nl/docs#/) addresses these last two concerns, by (1) making provision for hosting Rule collections not in scope or rejected by SPDX, and (2) doing so in an otherwise compatible schema in a Github repository. The service is already available, and extends the SPDX functionally by providing additional API methods that are useful \- such as obtaining legal, machine, and human-readable representations of the same licence directly.

The EOSC Beyond project will integrate the OpenREL registry with the EDEN Licence Facade Service, using its API calls to register new **Policies**, and using its IRIs to reference **Policies**, **Licences**, **Access** Conditions, and **Process** Rules.

# 4\. Schema Definition

*This section is **normative**.*

## 4.1 NameSpace Definition

Table 4.1.1 provides a definition of and rules for the OpenREL namespace.

*Table 4.1.1. OpenREL Namespace Definition*

| \# | Label | Description | Reference |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 4.1.1-01 | Namespace prefix  | https\://w3id.org/openrel/ |  |
| 4.1.1-02 | Target URL | The OpenREL registry MUST be implemented as a GitHib repository, typically as defined below: https\://github.com/wimhugo/openrel |  |
| 4.1.1-03 | Redirection | Redirection MUST be defined in .htaccess |  |
| 4.1.1-04 | Subspaces | The OpenREL registry MUST implement a number of sub-namespaces as data folders (subspaces). These serve as IRI targets for the following classes: Agents (openrel:agent.IRI) Rules (openrel:rule.IRI) Asset Collections (openrel:assetcol.IRI) Policies (openrel:policy.IRI) Licences (openrel:licence.IRI) Access Conditions (openrel:access.IRI) Process Rules (openrel:process.IRI) Constraints (openrel:constraint.IRI) Actions (openrel:action.IRI) |  |
| 4.1.1-05 | Subspace recognition and redirection | Subspace redirection MUST be based on regex patterns corresponding to the subspace label, and redirect to the appropriate target folder in the Github repository. |  |
| 4.1.1-06 | Content negotiation | Content negotiation adds qualifiers to Policy IRIs, and MUST be implemented as follows: openrel:policy.IRI/original Same as text/html openrel:policy.IRI/json Same as application/json openrel:policy.IRI/machine Same as application/json-ld openrel:policy.IRI/legal Same as text/plain |  |
| 4.1.1-07 | Repository Curators | GitHub usernames responsible for the namespace MUST be defined. |  |
| 4.1.1-08 | Owning organisation  | [EOSC Beyond Project](https://www.eosc-beyond.eu/) MUST maintain the repository, and SHOULD transfer the repository to a suitable EOSC node at the completion of the project |  |
| 4.1.1-09 | Change control process | Change management MUST be done via pull request–based updates and additions. |  |
| 4.1.1-10 | Namespace structure | The Git repository hosting the namespace data MUST implement the following minimum folder structure: |  |
|  | openrel/ ├── configs/ │   └── ontology/ │   │   └── openrel-core.ttl │   └── shacl/ │   │   └── openrel-shapes.ttl │   └── templates/ │   │   └── jsonld/ │   │       ├── policy-template.jsonld │   │       ├── rule-template.jsonld │   │       ├── actor-template.jsonld │   │       └── \<more\>.jsonld │   └── vocabs/ │      └── openrel/ │      │   ├── policy-types.ttl │      │   ├── rule-types.ttl │      │   ├── relation-types.ttl │      │   └── \<more\>-type.ttl │      └── odrl/ ├── examples/ │   ├── example-policy.jsonld │   ├── example-licence.jsonld │   ├── example-rule.jsonld │   ├── example-actor.jsonld ├── data/ │   ├── agent/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<agentIRI\>.jsonld │   ├── rule/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<ruleIRI\>.jsonld │   ├── policy/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<policyIRI\>.jsonld │   ├─licence/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<licenceIRI\>.jsonld │   ├──access/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<accessIRI\>.jsonld │   ├──process/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<processIRI\>.jsonld │   ├──constraint/ │   │   ├── index.json │   │   └── \<constraintIRI\>.jsonld │   └──action/ │       ├── index.json │       └── \<repositoryIRI\>.jsonld ├── graph/ │   └── openrel.jsonld ├── test/ │   ├── index.json │   └── \<objectIRI\>.jsonld └── import/     └── import-all.ttl |  |  |
| 4.1.1-11 | Versioning mechanism | Amendments to IRI-referenced objects are versioned, and a new version of an existing IRI object, based on an accepted pull request, MUST Create a copy of the previous version with a version-appended file name; Retain the same IRI and filename in the Git repository for the new version; Record a new version number based on the versioning syntax guidelines; Reference the previous version in the appropriate element; Record a date-time stamp for the new version. |  |
| 4.1.1-12 | Versioning Syntax | The versioning syntax MUST follow the following guideline: Major changes are recorded as a full version number increment, e.g. version j.n becomes version (j+1).1. Major changes involve semantic changes to the properties of the object itself. Minor changes are recorded as a minor version increment, e.g. version j.n becomes version j.(n+1). Minor changes involve typographical corrections to object properties and additions or changes to its relations. |  |
| 4.1.1-13 | SKOS Definitions | The schema MUST implement SKOS-based (TTL) definitions of objects, vocabularies, and relationships |  |
| 4..1.1-14 | SHACL Definitions | The schema MUST implement SHACL constraints to define the shape of objects and constraints on its cardinality and relations. |  |

## 4.2 IRI Structure, Use of Subclasses, and Vocabularies

The Classes, Subclasses, Vocabularies (Concept Schemes), and IRIs used in the OpenREL vocabulary will follow the specifications defined in 

*Table 4.2.1. OpenREL IRI, Class, Subclass, and Vocabulary Rules*

| \# | Aspect | Description | Reference |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 4.2.1-01 | IRI Structure | Based on the structure defined in 4.1.1-04 (Subspaces), an IRI MUST consist of the following components: openrel:\<classname\>.\<identifier\> |  |
| 4.2.1-02 | Identifiers | Identifiers MUST be computed as a random combination of 8 lowercase characters and digits. |  |
| 4.2.1-03 | Identifier Algorithm | Algorithm: A random value is generated as an integer between 0 and 9 trillion This value is converted to base 36 with a limit of 8 characters.  Collision probability is low, with a possible 4.2 trillion combinations. This algorithm SHOULD be used since it can easily be computed in spreadsheets without access to hash functions, but any other algorithm producing the same output of random character string MAY be used. |  |
| 4.2.1-03 | Classes and Subclasses | The following decision rules apply to definition of classes and subclasses: All classes are implemented by preference as subclasses of the following classes that are already defined in ***general*** ontologies. e.g.: owl:Thing dcat: classes schema: classes dct: classes A new class is a distinct entity that cannot be implemented as a subclass of an existing class. A subclass must extend the properties of a class, if its only property is a distinct type of the same class, a vocabulary must be used to describe the types and a property added to the class.		 |  |
| 4.2.1-04 | Vocabularies and Code Lists | These are implemented as one of a number of semantic artefacts, with the following subtypes: **Code List:** An unordered list with no relations to other instances in the list except shared typology. **Vocabulary (Concept Scheme)**: An unordered list of shared typology terms, with skos: and owl: based relations to other terms in external ontologies, as well as additional properties (definition, references, …) **Taxonomy (Concept Scheme)**: An unordered list but with hierarchical relations between instances of the same typology, possible relations to other vocabularies and ontologies, and additional properties (definition, references, …).  | \[2\] |

## 4.3 Relationship to Existing Standards and Vocabularies

Several resources must or should be reused in the definition of OpenREL, but the manner in which they are referenced and reused will be different.

*Table 4.3.1. Mechanisms for Reuse of Existing Resources*

| \# | Resource Type | Description | Reference |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 4.3.1-01 | Foundational to RDF | These resources include RDF, SKOS, SHACL, and OWL, and MUST be used to structure and link concepts and schemes in the OpenREL vocabulary.  If equivalence or reuse is considered, the following construct MUST be used, with frdf: representing the prefix for any of the foundational resources: openrel:\<someclass\> a \<frdf\>:\<class\> |  |
| 4.3.1-02 | Foundational to RDMI | Dublin Core, [schema.org](http://schema.org),  and DCAT/ DCAT-AP can be considered to represent foundations of research data management ontology, and these classes and vocabularies SHOULD be reused without creation of new classes or concept schemes whenever possible. If equivalence or reuse is considered, the following construct MUST be used, with rdmi: representing the prefix for any of the foundational resources: openrel:\<someclass\> a \<rdmi\>:\<class\> |  |
| 4.3.1-03 | Foundational to Rights Encoding | Similarly, ODRL and ccREL are foundational to rights expression, and MUST be implemented in a similar way: openrel:\<someclass\> a odrl:\<class\> openrel:\<someclass\> a ccrel:\<class\> |  |
| 4.3.1-04 | Other Rights-Related Resources | Other resources that are applicable, such as DALICC and ISDA Core are not used as foundational classes, but mappings are provided as properties of the OpenREL classes.  Implementation MUST follow the following example property assertions: openrel:\<someclass\> skos:exactMatch dalicc:\<class\>, or any other skos:\<relation\> that is contextually relevant. |  |
| 4.3.1-05 | Other Common Resources | Some resources are commonly used in the same landscape, such as FOAF, PROV, DPV, and others \- these are usually reserved for specific properties or class types and MAY be  implemented as required. |  |
| 4.3.1-06 | Profiles | For some resources, such as DALICC, ISDA Core, and ODRL, full correspondence SHOULD be documented (a Profile), enabling the export of an OpenREL Policy instance encoded in the vocabulary of the Profile. |  |

1\. Design Input: ChatGPT

This work is about a different namespace called ‘**openrel’**, not related to the previous work on PIDs or on repositories. It extends ODRL with refinements to describe licences, etc. 

The main classes are the following

1. Rules \- as defined in ODRL  
2. Subclasses of Rules as defined in ODRL \- Permissions, Duties, and Prohibitions  
3. Constraints \- as defined in ODRL  
4. Actions \- as defined in ODRL  
5. Assets and Asset Collections \- as defined in ODRL  
6. Parties and Party Collections \- as defined in ODRL   
   1. Refinement: Party Collections have subclasses corresponding to Agents defined elsewhere, for example. in DCAT  
7. Policies \- as defined in ODRL  
   1. Refinement: Policies have four new subclasses defined in the openrel namespace  
      1. Policy (explicitly a policy)  
      2. Licence (rules for intellectual property)  
      3. Access (rules for access duties and prohibitions, but could include permissions)  
      4. Process (process-related rules)  
8. A new class defined in the openrel namespace \- Rule Collection \- that can have up to four sections, each describing one or more Policy Subclasses (Policy, Licence, Access, Process), and these descriptions can indicate a number of rules organised by Permissions, Duties, and Prohibitions, as does the ODRL Policy, or it can point to (reference) any other ODRL Policy or openrel Rule Collection.  
9. The openrel namespace have a set of vocabularies to ensure proper identification of   
   1. Policy subclasses: Policy, Licence, Access, Process  
   2. Rule subclasses: Permissions, Duties, Prohibitions  
   3. Relationships: see CYPHER encoding below.  
   4. There may be more

The task is to create a set of files describing the schema for the above (ODRL extended by openrel) using SKOS TTL for classes, subclasses, and vocabularies, and using SHACL to define the shape of classes and cardinality constraints for relationships between them. Many of these will already exist as resources to support ODRL and could then be extended to include openrel classes and subclasses.

Parsing JSON

JSON files may have a hierarchy with sub-elements and sub-sub-elements. In such a case, a row is generated for each element in the deepest nesting in the hierarchy. However, JSON files can also contain arrays in sub-elements and sub-sub-elements. Is it not simpler to write a routine to analyse the JSON structure and then suggest a mapping and template for the CSV output? The objective is to 'flatten' the JSON. 1. Start with a set of files that define  
   1. Classes and properties in SKOS TTL, even if these are just placeholders (empty files)  
   2. Constraints and other shape information in SHACL files

The free text is obtained from a text file available in a github repository.  
4. The current schema (1) is compared to the free text description in (3) and a set of proposed changes to (1) is created as pull requests in the GitHub repository. This way, the curator of the schema can preview the changes before accepting them

I need to design a set of SKOS-like TTL files with SHACL constraints to model the following:

1. Work with three main classes:  
   1. “Attributes”, “Repositories”, and “Services”. Each of these represent a set of nodes in a graph, and can have several properties unique to the specific entity.   
   2. Many of these properties will be well-known (e.g. dct:title, etc.) but some of the properties are defined in a new namespace (trsp).  
2. There are relationships between Repositories or Services and Attributes:  
   1. ‘Profiles’ represent a specific type of relationship between these entities, for example a profile for a specific attribute will list an array of applicable repositories and/or services.   
   2. Each relationship should indicate the graph node IRI for the service or repository, and the graph node IRI for the attribute.  
   3. Profiles can have a type property based on a controlled vocabulary (e.g. ‘Repository’, ‘Service’ (which are equivalent to the entities above).  
   4. The relationship can have additional properties, again based on well-known namespaces and trap-specific properties.  
   5. But \- there are also additional profiles that are not repositories or services, and reference a Linked Open Data IRI from an external web resource. These profiles can be of type ‘Source’, ‘Standard’, ‘Community Profile’, ‘User Profile’, and so on, adding to the type vocabulary.

A natural language representation of a proposed structure looks like this:

namespaces (context) in use \- apply to the structure as applicable

- skos  
- [schema.org](http://schema.org)  
- dct \- dublin core  
- shacl  
- rdf  
- xsd  
- dcat and dcat-ap

properties (a vocabulary of trsp properties)

- id (iri) (a trsp namespace property  
- label and language  
- alternative label and language  
- an array of additional linked open data iri’s defined elsewhere, such as wikidata  
  - id iri  
  - usage (one of ‘default’ or no value, if an external iri is marked as default it is preferred over the trsp namespace iri for the property).  
- array of annotations and web references  
  - iri (some external irl or compact identifier in most cases)

profile types (a trsp vocabulary)

- values ‘Repository’, ‘Service’, ‘Source’, ‘Standard’, ‘Community Profile’, ‘User Profile’  
- local (trsp) iri for each value  
- description for each value  
- one or more external (linked open data) iri as applicable

measurement types (a trsp vocabulary)

- values ‘None \- no constraints’, ‘Binary’, ‘Binary with Evidence’, ‘Vocabulary’, ‘Registry’, ‘Checklist’, ‘Formats’, Standard’,  ‘Specification’  
- local (trsp) iri for each value  
- description for each value  
- one or more external (linked open data) iri as applicable

repository

- id (iri) (trsp namespace) \- for example trsp:repo.668467EC38  
- title and language  
- alternative title and language  
- other well-known or trsp properties  
- array of applicable attributes  
  - attribute iri  
  - value  
  - date of measurement  
  - attribute-specific provenance properties, such as which test was used to determine the value or where it was harvested from. This is a linked open data iri.  
- array of applicable services  
  - service iri  
  - relationship type, which is equivalent to ‘service is offered by repository x’ or ‘service is used by repository x’.   
- array of annotations and web references  
  - iri (some external irl or compact identifier in most cases)

service

- id (iri) (trsp namespace) \- for example trsp:serv.B89FC1EE2D  
- title and language  
- alternative title and language  
- other well-known or trsp properties  
- array of applicable attributes  
  - attribute iri  
  - value  
  - date of measurement  
  - attribute-specific provenance properties, such as which test was used to determine the value or which source it was harvested from. This is a linked open data iri.  
- array of annotations and web references  
  - iri (some external irl or compact identifier in most cases)

profile

- id (iri) (trsp namespace) \- can be a repository (example trsp:repo.668467EC38), a service (example trsp:serv.B89FC1EE2D, or an external linked open data iri.  
- title and language  
- alternative title and language  
- profile type (from controlled vocabulary, see above)  
- array of annotations and web references  
  - iri (some external irl or compact identifier in most cases)

attribute

- id (iri) (trsp namespace \- example trsp:att.0AB11676B0)  
- label and language  
- alternative label and language  
- description and language  
- keyword (a dcat property, might be replaced by a skos relationship later on \- skos:broader)  
- measurement type (a value form a vocabulary \- see above)  
- benchmark (a trsp property that depends on the measurement type)  
- cardinality (which can be 0..1, 1..1, 0..n, 1..n), could be a shacl minvalue/ maxvalue  
- an array of additional linked open data iri’s (alternate identifiers) defined elsewhere, such as schema.org  
  - id (iri)  
  - usage (one of ‘default’ or no value, if an external iri is marked as default it is preferred over the trsp namespace iri for the attribute).  
- an array of applicable profiles  
  - profile iri (from the trsp namespace)  
  - profile label (duplication but improves human readability)  
  - keyword (a dcat property, might be replaced by a skos relationship later on \- skos:broader)  
  - measurement type (a value form a vocabulary \- see above)  
  - benchmark (a trsp property that depends on the measurement type)

Task 1 is to create a SHACL/TTL-based set of schemas and constraints for the structure above.

Task 2 is then to create JSON-LD and SKOS templates for each of the above, with empty placeholders for the property values (“”).
